solution:
from typing import List


def longest_increasing_subsequence(nums: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """ Return a longest strictly increasing subsequence of nums.
    A subsequence keeps the original order of the elements it takes but may
    skip any of them; strictly increasing means every element is greater than
    the one before it, so equal values never both appear.
    When several longest strictly increasing subsequences exist, return the
    one whose list of values is lexicographically smallest (compare the first
    values, then the second values, and so on). Return [] for an empty list.
    Values may be negative and may be as large as the 64-bit signed integer
    range allows; do not rely on sentinel values.
    >>> longest_increasing_subsequence([3, 1, 2, 1, 8, 5, 6])
    [1, 2, 5, 6]
    >>> longest_increasing_subsequence([5, 4, 3])
    [3]
    """
    n = len(nums)
    if n == 0:
        return []
    # best[i]: length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence starting at i
    best = [1] * n
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if nums[j] > nums[i] and best[j] + 1 > best[i]:
                best[i] = best[j] + 1
    need = max(best)
    out = []
    pos = -1
    prev = None
    while need > 0:
        # among positions that can start the rest, take the smallest value,
        # and its earliest position, which leaves the most choices afterwards
        pick = -1
        for j in range(pos + 1, n):
            if best[j] == need and (prev is None or nums[j] > prev):
                if pick == -1 or nums[j] < nums[pick]:
                    pick = j
        out.append(nums[pick])
        prev = nums[pick]
        pos = pick
        need -= 1
    return out
